cars.variant: VH R/T E49 — November 1972 Australian four-speed road-test reference
cars.specification_market: November 1972 Wheels E49 road test, republished 15 February 2026. Native published bhp, lb-ft and cubic inches are retained; no net/gross standard or metric conversion is invented. This is the six-cylinder E49 with four-speed manual, not the accompanying 340-cubic-inch E55 V8 automatic. Conflicting maximum-speed/rpm shorthand, later technical retellings, factory superlatives and acceleration conversions are excluded. E37/E38/E49, later styling series and V8 derivatives do not add extra original-family counts.
cars.summary: The E49 Charger demonstrated that a developed six-cylinder engine could contend at the top of Australia’s muscle-car field. Its four-speed gearbox and revised axle gearing made its performance more accessible than the earlier three-speed E38. Contemporary Wheels driving praised its open-road balance and rapid response, while recording brake fade. That distinctive six-cylinder performance identity merits one original Charger family entry.

cars.generation: Original LC/LJ compact six-cylinder XU-1 production-road performance family
cars.variant: LC GTR XU-1 — original 1970 factory brochure reference
cars.specification_market: Original LC brochure with 1970 GMH copyright imprint; both scanned pages rendered and visually read. Its 3048 cc and native gross power/torque are retained exactly, not replaced by a 3100 badge or later 202/3.3-litre LJ figures. The optional 3.08 axle is not standard; no unprinted gearbox detail, modified museum-car hardware, overall production total or race tune is inferred. LC and LJ are grouped into one original compact XU-1 programme; the existing LX A9X is a distinct later platform.
cars.summary: Holden’s compact six-cylinder XU-1 offered a focused alternative to Australia’s large performance cars. The original LC package combined a reworked head and camshaft, triple carburettors, limited-slip differential, revised suspension and aerodynamic aids. Its broader LC/LJ programme became central to Australian touring-car history. This coordinated engineering and sporting heritage justify one original XU-1 family entry, separate from the later LX A9X.

cars.generation: XA/XB/XC Australian Falcon production-road performance body generation
cars.variant: XB GT Hardtop automatic — January 1974 Australian road-test reference
cars.specification_market: January 1974 Wheels road test, republished 26 August 2016. The selected Hardtop has automatic transmission and power steering; the accompanying manual sedan has a different imported engine and steering specification. The public excerpt supports the listed engine reference, braking and chassis fields but not a precise power figure or automatic gear count. 4V/2V engine terminology is not a valve-count claim. XA/XB/XC, sedan/hardtop, Cobra and appearance editions do not become separate counts here. No film-car modifications, race hardware or optional sunroof is treated as standard.
cars.summary: The XB GT advanced the Australian Falcon GT tradition with four-wheel disc brakes and substantial chassis refinement. Period long-distance driving strongly praised its braking, while criticising the automatic Hardtop’s light steering, body rattles and restricted visibility. Together with the XB GT programme’s documented touring-car championship heritage, this gives the distinct 1970s body generation a clear performance-history case beyond the earlier XY.
